The story changed here

Unexpected Findings That Changed the Story

The clusters were useful—but the most valuable moments came when the data contradicted the simple story. Two patterns shifted the analysis from describing users to identifying practical intervention points.

Finding 01 · Context hiding in plain sight
Device preference unexpectedly mapped onto behavioral profiles.
Evidence
  • C1 repeatedly favored tablet; C2 was predominantly mobile.
  • C3 combined TV, long-form content, and multi-device behavior.
  • C4 was primarily desktop-based.
  • Those device patterns remained stable across weeks.
Interpretation

Device choice appeared to reflect the context in which exercise fit into a user’s life—structured at-home routines, short mobile sessions, immersive TV workouts, or desktop-based exploration.

Business Use

Preferred device could serve as an early, low-cost signal for cold-start segmentation—not as a cluster label, but as a starting hypothesis. TSS could personalize onboarding, content recommendations, and initial messaging, then refine the segment as behavioral history develops.

Finding 02 · The quiet majority
The least active group held the greatest activation potential.
55% of usersHighest challenge uplift63.2% post-challenge retention
Evidence

C2 was the largest segment and had the lowest total viewing and consistency. Yet it responded most strongly during the challenge. The sharpest gap appeared afterward, when retention fell to 63.2%.

Interpretation

The challenge proved that these users were reachable. Their drop-off came when temporary motivation ended without a continuing routine to carry it forward.

Business Use · Build a post-challenge bridge
Immediate follow-upMobile-first quickiesShort repeat challengesConsistency reminders

Cluster 2 is highly responsive to activation. The retention opportunity lies in helping that initial response develop into a repeatable habit.

Learning analytics · Team project

What student behavior can—and cannot—predict

Using event-level data from Carnegie Learning’s MATHia platform, our team investigated whether patterns inside an online math tutor could predict three different outcomes: math knowledge, metacognition, and motivation.

Python / RXGBoostFeature engineeringRepeated train-test splitsCross-validationModel interpretation

Research question

Can the way a student works through problems reveal not only what they learn, but also how they monitor learning and sustain motivation?

Behavioral features

We summarized session frequency, time and actions per workspace, hint timing, help intensity, error correction, mastery progress, and task completion.

Model design

We trained separate XGBoost models because each outcome had a different measurement structure. Math knowledge used regression; metacognition and motivation used ordinal classification.

Validation

Cross-validation guided model complexity and early stopping. Repeated train-test splits tested whether the psychological-outcome results were stable or dependent on a lucky split.

What worked

Behavioral logs carried a strong signal for later math performance. In-progress performance, persistence, and help use gave the model useful information about learning.

What did not

The same logs were far less informative for metacognition and motivation. That inconclusive result suggested that internal states cannot be recovered reliably from clicks alone.

Practical direction

A math-performance model could support early educator alerts. Psychological outcomes need richer evidence, such as short self-reports or measures designed to capture affect and cognition directly.
